scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that outside knowledge drives progress while arguing 'no field' is too absolute; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Many great breakthroughs happen when two different fields meet and share ideas.
Some people argue that no field of study can advance significantly unless it incorporates knowledge from outside that field.
I agree that outside knowledge often drives progress, but I believe the word no makes the claim too absolute.

sections.role: Body 1 — How outside knowledge drives progress

sentences.text: First, borrowing knowledge from other fields often leads to major advances.
Ideas and tools from one subject can solve problems that another could not crack alone.
For example, biology advanced enormously once it began using the methods of chemistry and physics.
This shows that combining fields can open doors that a single discipline cannot.
Fresh ideas from outside can also break the fixed habits that hold a field back.
Many modern fields, such as computer science, were born from blending several disciplines.
To this extent, the claim captures a real and important truth.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why 'no field' is too absolute

sentences.text: Second, however, the claim that no field can advance without outside knowledge goes too far.
Some progress comes from working deeply within a single field's own ideas and methods.
Consider a mathematician who solves a long-standing problem using only the tools of mathematics itself.
Such achievements show that a field can sometimes advance significantly on its own.
Deep focus within one subject can produce discoveries that broad borrowing never would.
Outside knowledge is often helpful, but it is not always strictly necessary for progress.
Advance, then, can come both from blending fields and from deep work within one.
In conclusion, incorporating outside knowledge often drives a field forward.
But some fields advance significantly through deep work within their own boundaries.
Progress comes both from crossing the borders between fields and from digging deep within them.
